routine.title: A regular routine
routine.context: You are telling a friend about your usual day.

breakfast.explanation: This is a habit, not what is on your spoon right now.

walk.explanation: This is your usual way to get to school; you could be at home now.

facts.title: How familiar things work
facts.context: A child asks about animals and the shop's closing time.

shop.explanation: You are giving the shop's usual scheduled closing time.

sleep.explanation: This is a general observation about cats, not what one cat is doing right now.

contrast.explanation: The first sentence describes a habit. The second describes a game in progress now.

finished.title: A finished day
finished.context: At home, you are describing what happened yesterday after school.

park.translation: We played in the park yesterday.
park.explanation: You place the game in yesterday's finished day, without focusing on a moment inside it.

soup.explanation: Making soup was an event last night.

story.title: Telling a sequence
story.context: A friend asks how your walk went on Saturday.

rain.translation: It started to rain, so we went home.
rain.explanation: You name two finished events in sequence.

friend.translation: I met Anna and gave her the book.
friend.explanation: In your story, meeting Anna and giving her the book happen one after another.

contrast.second: I have lost my key. I cannot open the door.
contrast.explanation: The first tells what happened yesterday. The second focuses on the missing key now.

decision.title: A decision or promise now
decision.context: Your friend's hands are full and the phone rings. You decide to help.

phone.explanation: You decide what to do in response to the situation.

bag.explanation: You offer help and promise to take the bag.

prediction.title: What you expect tomorrow
prediction.context: You discuss tomorrow's outing and what you think will happen.

weather.translation: I think it will be sunny tomorrow.
weather.explanation: You give your prediction about the weather.

game.explanation: Knowing your friend's tastes, you predict their reaction.

contrast.second: I am meeting Anna at five.
contrast.explanation: The first is a decision made now. The second is an arrangement already made. Will is not the only way to talk about the future.

now.title: Look at what is happening
now.context: You look into the kitchen and out into the garden right now.

dinner.explanation: Cooking is happening now; dinner is still being prepared.

ball.explanation: You see the game in progress rather than describe a habit.

arranged.title: An arrangement already made
arranged.context: You check your plans: the meeting is arranged and the tickets are bought.

meeting.translation: I am meeting Leo after school tomorrow.
meeting.explanation: The meeting is in the future, but you have already arranged it.

cinema.translation: We are going to the cinema on Friday.
cinema.explanation: This is an arrangement for Friday, not an action happening now.

contrast.second: She is reading on the sofa now.
contrast.explanation: The first is her usual evening routine. The second is what she is doing now.

background.title: What was happening then
background.context: A friend called yesterday at seven. You recall what you were doing.

dinner.translation: I was eating dinner when you called.
dinner.explanation: The call came in the middle of dinner; you had started eating and had not finished.

window.translation: It was raining when I left school.
window.explanation: Rain is the background at the moment you leave, not a separate step in the story.

parallel.title: Two activities at once
parallel.context: You describe yesterday evening at home when everyone was busy.

family.translation: I was drawing while Dad was cooking.
family.explanation: Drawing and cooking were both in progress at the same time.

bedtime.translation: At eight, my sister was reading and I was brushing my teeth.
bedtime.explanation: It is like a snapshot of two activities at eight o'clock.

contrast.second: I was cooking dinner at six.
contrast.explanation: The first reports cooking dinner as an event. The second places you in the middle of cooking at six, without saying when you finished.

futureMoment.title: A look into tomorrow
futureMoment.context: A friend suggests calling at seven tomorrow. You explain what you will be doing.

dinner.translation: At seven tomorrow, we will be eating dinner.
dinner.explanation: You picture a moment in the middle of tomorrow's dinner.

bus.translation: At this time tomorrow, I will be travelling home.
bus.explanation: At that future moment, the journey will still be in progress.

expected.title: An expected activity
expected.context: You prepare for Saturday's party and discuss everyone's morning tasks.

cake.translation: I will be baking the cake all morning on Saturday.
cake.explanation: The focus is on the activity that will occupy the morning.

garden.translation: The children will be playing in the garden while we set the table.
garden.explanation: You picture their future game as the background to setting the table.

contrast.first: I will call you at six.
contrast.second: At six, I will be walking home.
contrast.explanation: The first promises a call. The second describes an activity that will be in progress at six.

result.title: It happened earlier and matters now
result.context: You are at the door or about to eat: the result matters now.

key.translation: I have lost my key. I cannot get in.
key.explanation: You do not say when the key was lost; what matters is that it is missing now.

hands.translation: I have washed my hands. I am ready to eat.
hands.explanation: Your hands are clean now, so you are ready to eat.

experience.title: Things you have experienced
experience.context: You discuss experiences in your lives up to now, without giving a date.

sea.explanation: You say that this experience is part of your life up to now.

sushi.explanation: You ask about experience up to now, not a particular dinner.

contrast.first: I saw the sea last summer.
contrast.explanation: The first refers to a finished time last summer. The second reports an experience up to today.

before.title: What had happened earlier
before.context: You got home yesterday at six and found dinner already prepared.

cooking.translation: Mum had cooked dinner before we got home.
cooking.explanation: Mum finished cooking first; you arrived later. You look back from that past arrival.

homework.translation: I had finished my homework before my friend arrived.
homework.explanation: The homework was already finished when your friend arrived.

explanation.title: Why something happened then
explanation.context: You describe yesterday's outing and explain a surprise.

missed.translation: The film had started when we reached the cinema.
missed.explanation: The film started before your arrival; that is why you were late.

forgot.translation: I could not open the door because I had left my key at school.
forgot.explanation: You could not get in later; leaving the key at school happened earlier.

contrast.first: When I arrived, Dad cooked dinner.
contrast.second: When I arrived, Dad had cooked dinner.
contrast.explanation: In the first, cooking follows the arrival. In the second, dinner is ready by the arrival. Past Perfect is not required in every story when the order is already clear.

deadline.title: Finished by a deadline
deadline.context: You promise to finish things before the guests arrive tonight.

room.translation: I will have cleaned my room by six.
room.explanation: You picture six o'clock with the cleaning already finished.

cake.translation: We will have made the cake before the guests arrive.
cake.explanation: The guests' arrival is the future point by which the cake will be ready.

lookBack.title: Looking back from the future
lookBack.context: You plan a long trip and discuss what will be behind you by tomorrow evening.

home.translation: By tomorrow evening, we will have reached home.
home.explanation: You look back from tomorrow evening at a journey that will be complete.

book.translation: By the end of the trip, I will have read this book.
book.explanation: At the end of the trip, the reading will be complete, not still in progress.

contrast.first: At six, I will be cleaning my room.
contrast.second: By six, I will have cleaned my room.
contrast.explanation: In the first, cleaning is in progress at six. In the second, it is finished by six.

still.title: Started earlier and still going
still.context: You are still waiting for a friend or doing homework and say how long it has lasted.

wait.translation: I have been waiting for you for twenty minutes.
wait.explanation: Waiting started earlier and is still going on; its duration matters.

study.translation: We have been doing our homework since four.
study.explanation: You are still working now; four o'clock is when you started.

evidence.title: Just stopped, with signs still visible
evidence.context: You come home wet and your friend has flour on their hands.

rain.translation: I have been walking in the rain. My coat is wet.
rain.explanation: The walk may have ended; your wet coat shows the recent activity now.

baking.translation: She has been baking. There is flour on her hands.
baking.explanation: You are explaining signs of recent activity, not counting finished cakes.

contrast.second: I have been making sandwiches for half an hour.
contrast.explanation: The first focuses on the completed result and number. The second focuses on the activity and duration, without saying how many are ready.

durationBefore.title: How long before that moment
durationBefore.context: Your friend finally arrived yesterday at six. You say how long you had waited before that.

waiting.translation: I had been waiting for half an hour when Leo arrived.
waiting.explanation: You measure the waiting up to Leo's past arrival, not up to now.

playing.translation: We had been playing for an hour when Mum called us in.
playing.explanation: The game had lasted an hour by Mum's call; the focus is on its duration.

pastEvidence.title: Explaining past tiredness or mess
pastEvidence.context: You remember how you found your friend yesterday after an outing.

running.translation: He was tired because he had been running.
running.explanation: The tiredness was then; the earlier running explains that past state.

painting.translation: Her hands were blue because she had been painting a picture.
painting.explanation: You explain blue hands in the past by the recent activity before that moment.

contrast.first: When Mum came, I had done my homework.
contrast.second: When Mum came, I had been doing my homework for an hour.
contrast.explanation: In the first, the work is finished by Mum's arrival. In the second, we know how long you worked, without claiming it was finished.

futureWait.title: Waiting for a train
futureWait.context: The train is delayed. You started waiting at five and discuss the duration by seven.

train.translation: By seven, we will have been waiting for two hours.
train.explanation: You count the waiting from five to the future point at seven, without saying the train will arrive then.

queue.translation: When the doors open at noon, I will have been standing in this queue for an hour.
queue.explanation: You have been queuing since eleven; you count one hour up to the future opening time.

milestone.title: A future anniversary
milestone.context: You have been doing something for a while and picture a future anniversary.

school.translation: By next June, I will have been learning English for three years.
school.explanation: Learning has already started; you count its duration by next June.

team.translation: By the end of this season, she will have been playing for our team for five years.
team.explanation: She is already on the team; by the future season's end, her playing time will total five years.

contrast.first: At seven, we will be waiting at the station.
contrast.second: By seven, we will have been waiting for two hours.
contrast.explanation: The first shows an activity at seven. The second also tells how long it will have lasted by then. This long form serves that focus; it is not required for everyday plans.

futurePerfectContinuous.note: This form is uncommon. It is useful when duration up to a future point matters; a simpler sentence is often enough in everyday conversation.
